title: Title
paras: Hi, I'm Vlad. Welcome, and thanks to Haufe for the room.
Tonight is about people who now build alone what used to take a whole team. Real examples, with real numbers. And I'll start with my own, which is a bit embarrassing.

title: AGENTIC.tm
paras: Two communities put this evening together. The first one is AGENTIC.tm. We're the people on the shop floor: how code actually gets made with AI. Meetups, demos, Cafe Cursor, and a few evenings that were mostly beer.

title: Indie TM
paras: The second one is Indie TM. That's the shop window: people who build products and sell them, and tell you the real numbers. What worked, and what didn't.
For a long time these were two different conversations. In the last year, they turned into the same one. That's why we're in one room tonight.

title: How the evening goes
paras: Here's the plan. I talk for about fifteen minutes. At seven, Raul. Then a short break. At quarter to eight, Mircea. Then drinks.
House rules: no pitching, real numbers, and you can ask questions anytime. Interrupt them, they agreed to it.

title: 2024 vs 2026
paras: So, my embarrassing example.
In 2024, this is how I used AI. Emails. LinkedIn posts. "I'm humbled to announce." I'm not proud of it.
In 2026, the same kind of model does this. It logs in, finds my invoices, downloads them, and sends them to my accountant. Same model family. Light years apart.
I won't tell you why yet. Just look at the distance.

title: Text became action
paras: Here's what changed. Look at the left. Ask a chatbot "why did our signups drop" and you get this: "Signups can drop for many reasons, seasonality..." Text. Correct, and useless.
Now give the same model a terminal. It reads, it decides, it runs one command, it reads the result, it decides again.
It queries PostHog: signups down 38 percent, on mobile.
It reads the logs: 500 errors on /signup.
It greps the code: signup.ts, line 42.
It deploys a fix. Signups come back.
Four steps. Each one depends on what the last one found. That's the whole trick. Text became action.

title: The garage
paras: And the toolbox kept growing.
2023: it could read, edit, and delete files. Code only.
2024: a shell. Now it can run things.
2025: a browser, and the whole computer. It clicks, scrolls, logs in.
Also 2025: MCP. It talks to your other systems: your analytics, your billing, your CRM.
2026: other agents. It hands work to its friends.
Here's the part people miss. The models are now trained, with reinforcement learning, directly on these loops. That's why it keeps getting better, month after month.
Let me show you.

title: The accountant
paras: This is a real message from my accountant. Every month. "Hi Vlad, could you send me this month's RunPod invoices, please?"
Every month I forget. So I gave it to a bot.

title: Demo 1, invoices
paras: It gets a cloud VM. Its own machine.
It opens a browser.
It logs in.
It finds the invoices and downloads them.
It writes the email and sends it.
That's the fun part. Now the scary part.

title: 2,000 PRs
paras: Tool use without verification is a junior with admin rights. Fast, confident, and sometimes very wrong.
So how do people run this at scale? Lauren Tan, in a talk this September: "last month I did something pretty crazy. I shipped 2,000 pull requests to production."
It doesn't work because the agent is careful. It works because of the environment around it.
One: the agent checks its own work.
Two: separate verifiers sign off the merge. Not the same agent.
Three: every mistake that happens twice becomes a rule in the environment. Not a note in a prompt. A rule.
Because if you keep writing the same instruction to the agent, the instruction is the symptom. The real fix lives in the environment.

title: Guardrails
paras: This is what that looks like. Deterministic guardrails. Small units, put together, checked by rules that don't have opinions.
The work goes through lint.
Then static analysis.
Then import rules: who is allowed to talk to whom.
Then tests.
Then a verifier on the pull request.
If you're a human, coding like this would be awful. You'd quit in a week. But the environment isn't built for us. It's built for the agent.

title: Demo 2, funnel to production
paras: Second demo. Same idea, bigger loop.
The bot pulls data from PostHog and Stripe.
It builds the funnel.
It finds where users drop off.
It proposes fixes and opens pull requests.
Five pull requests. And now each of them goes through the gates you just saw.

title: One role = one line
paras: So here's the bridge to the rest of the evening.
A role is three things. Context: what it needs to know. Tools: what it can touch. Verification: how you know it did it right.
Put that loop on repeat and you have a production line. One line for code. One for data. One for support. One for content.
The human doesn't do the work anymore. The human builds the environment, and runs several factories in parallel.
That's the one-person product team.

title: Handover
paras: And now, someone who actually lives this. Not my slides, the real thing.
The first Journey tonight. The story, the honest version. Please welcome Raul Popadineti.
